article.overview: A precision ranging system measures the distance between a spacecraft, lander or surface asset and a reference point, such as a ground station, a navigation satellite or another spacecraft, by timing signals or pulses that travel between them. On the Moon, accurate range measurements support orbit determination, surface navigation and geodesy, the study of the Moon's shape, gravity field and coordinate reference. The payload class is defined by its measurement function rather than by a single hardware design. This entry covers radio and laser ranging systems that have flown or are in development. The examples are the Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE), which carried out the first known demonstration of GNSS signal acquisition, tracking and navigation near the Moon [1]; the NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter laser ranging investigation [3]; and two ESA-linked lunar navigation developments, Moonlight and Lunar Pathfinder [4][5][6].
article.description: A precision ranging system combines a signal source or cooperative target, a radio or optical front end, an accurate clock or time reference, and processing that converts measured travel time into distance. There are two broad approaches. In a cooperative system, ground equipment sends a laser pulse or radio signal to a target that receives or returns it, and the time of flight gives the range. The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter laser ranging investigation works this way, with pulses fired from Earth and timed by the orbiter's instrument [3]. In a passive system, a receiver measures signals already transmitted by existing navigation satellites. LuGRE used this approach by tracking GPS and Galileo signals at lunar distances [1]. Planned lunar navigation infrastructure, such as ESA's Moonlight programme, would provide dedicated navigation signals from lunar orbit [4][5].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose is to determine where a spacecraft or surface asset is and how it is moving, with a precision sufficient for its task. NASA describes the LRO laser ranging investigation as meeting a precision orbit determination requirement, and as supporting a planned three-dimensional geodetic grid for the Moon built from surface spots measured by the LOLA instrument [3]. The LuGRE paper reports the first known demonstration of GNSS signal acquisition, tracking and navigation near the Moon, which shows that signals designed for Earth users can be used for navigation at lunar distances [1]. Applications include orbit determination for lunar spacecraft, navigation for landers and rovers, and timing and geodetic reference frames. Other applications depend on mission design and are not established by the sources reviewed for this article.
article.operating_principle:
Range is found from the time a signal takes to travel between two points: distance equals the speed of light multiplied by the travel time. For one-way laser ranging, the ground station fires a pulse at the orbiter, and the orbiter's receiver records the arrival time against a precise clock. NASA states that the LRO laser ranging investigation is intended to determine the spacecraft's position at a sub-meter level [3].

For a GNSS receiver, the satellite signal carries a known code. The receiver measures the delay of that code, called the pseudorange, and the phase of the carrier wave. A pseudorange includes the receiver clock error, so a navigation solution must estimate clock bias together with position. In general, carrier-phase measurements are much less noisy than code measurements but are ambiguous by whole wavelengths unless they are tracked continuously. In flight, LuGRE's code pseudorange noise was reported as roughly two orders of magnitude above its carrier-phase noise. The plotted values are not given as numbers in the text reviewed [1]. The receiver used a commercial clock whose frequency drift tracked temperature [1]. Position accuracy also depends on satellite geometry, which is expressed as dilution of precision (DOP) [7].
article.scientific_importance: Accurate range data tie spacecraft positions to a reference frame, which matters for interpreting lunar gravity and surface measurements. The LRO investigation's data also support lunar geodesy [3]. A lunar navigation service would provide position, navigation and timing from lunar orbit, which is the stated aim of ESA's Moonlight programme [4][5]. LuGRE's flight results show that terrestrial GNSS signals can be acquired and tracked at lunar distances, which informs the design of future lunar navigation systems [1]. The engineering value is therefore as much in the demonstrated performance envelope as in any single measurement.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for a precision ranging system. The values below describe specific flown, in-development or proposed hardware and must not be applied to the whole class. Where a figure is not in the sources reviewed, it is stated as not publicly specified.

examples.name: LuGRE (Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment, NASA and ASI, flown 2025)
examples.type: Flown lunar surface GNSS receiver payload
examples.description:
Type: flown hardware, operated on the lunar surface. LuGRE was a joint NASA and Italian Space Agency (ASI) payload. The receiver was developed by Qascom, with scientific support from Politecnico di Torino [1]. It flew on Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost Mission 1 lander, launched on 15 January 2025 and landed on 2 March 2025 at 08:34 UTC [1].

Receiver: Qascom QN400-SPACE, with two cold-redundant receiver modules under a supervisory board, a Xilinx Zynq 7000 baseband system-on-chip and an Analog Devices AD9361 RF front end [1]. Its antenna is a 3 by 3 planar, right-hand circularly polarised array with peak gain of 15.35 dBic on L1/E1 and 14.56 dBic on L5/E5. These are pre-flight chamber measurements [1]. The low-noise amplifier gains were 41.5 dB (L1/E1) and 44.2 dB (L5/E5), with noise figures of 0.8 dB and 1.3 dB, also pre-flight [1]. The mass, power and dimensions of the receiver alone are not stated [1].

Signals tracked: GPS L1 C/A and L5 (L5Q pilot channel), and Galileo E1 OS (E1C) and E5a (E5a-Q) [1].

Flight results reported: the first GNSS reception in lunar orbit was logged during operation OP23_0 [1]. The first lunar-surface navigation fix was obtained on 3 March 2025 at 06:51:35 UTC, when the receiver was about 356,237 km from Earth's surface [1]. The most distant fix was about 398,350 km on 16 March 2025, and the longest-range tracked signal was Galileo PRN 11 at 433,220 km [1]. Tracked signals spanned carrier-to-noise-density ratios (C/N0) of 18 to 48 dB-Hz. Flight GPS L1 C/N0 was generally 7 to 12 dB below the pre-flight prediction, and the cause is described as under investigation and not typical of lunar GNSS reception [1].

Operating totals: more than 111 hours cumulative, including more than 95 hours on the surface and more than 106 hours in real-time positioning mode [1]. The lander lost signal at 23:15 UTC on 16 March 2025, after a payload power loss at 22:50 UTC on the same day [1].

A pre-landing news report from February 2025 gave an in-orbit position error of about 1.5 km and a velocity error of about 2 m/s. That report does not state the basis or conditions for these values, and they are not surface accuracy figures [2].
examples.payload_mass_note: Complete LuGRE flight payload under 5 kg; receiver alone not stated.

flight_results.cn0_shortfall_vs_prediction_db: 7 to 12 below pre-flight prediction for GPS L1 (cause under investigation)

examples.name: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Laser Ranging (LR)
examples.type: Flown laser ranging hardware on LRO (archived reference page)
examples.status: flown; archived reference page last updated 2015; current operating status not stated
examples.description: Type: flown on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). The archived NASA page is marked for reference only and was last updated on 10 September 2015 [3]. Its function is that ground stations fire laser pulses at LRO. The flight hardware is a receiver telescope and fibre-optic cable on the LRO high-gain antenna, which route the signal to the LOLA instrument [3]. The ground hardware includes a pointable laser at a satellite laser ranging station, a data reception and distribution facility, and the LOLA Science Operations Center [3]. The page names NASA Goddard's NGSLR station, and other participating stations are not stated [3]. The stated accuracy is a sub-meter position level, with no numerical figure given [3]. The launch year, the current operating status, and the mass, power and dimensions of the hardware are not stated on the page [3]. This example overlaps with the separate laser ranging instrument entry in this catalogue (entry 185) and is included here as a ranging example.
examples.accuracy: sub-meter position level (no numerical figure stated)

examples.name: Moonlight navigation service (ESA, in development)
examples.type: Proposed lunar navigation and communications constellation
examples.description:
Type: proposed and in development, not flown. Moonlight is a navigation and communications constellation in lunar orbit rather than a single instrument [4]. A 2026 ESA and Telespazio programme status presentation could not be read as text in this run. Search-result summaries of it state that the navigation end-to-end chain passed its system preliminary design review, that the flight-model-ready target is 2028, and that the navigation performance goal is 10 m accuracy for at least 95% of the time over any 24 hours for real-time positioning [5]. These are programme targets, not measured performance.

Mass, power, dimensions and lifetime are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed [4][5].

programme_targets.navigation_performance_goal: 10 m accuracy for at least 95% of the time over any 24 h (real-time positioning)
programme_targets.basis: search-result summary of a 2026 ESA and Telespazio presentation; not verified against the PDF

examples.name: Lunar Pathfinder (ESA and SSTL, in development)
examples.type: Lunar orbit relay and navigation test payload
examples.status: in development; launch date and in-orbit results not confirmed
examples.description: Type: in development. The sources reviewed do not confirm a launch date or any in-orbit result [6]. The ranging-relevant hardware is a standard X-band transponder and a laser retroreflector, which allow tracking from Earth by laser ranging stations [6]. Its navigation purpose is to test reception of Galileo and GPS signals in lunar orbit. Planning sources from 2021 to 2022 projected a positioning accuracy of around 100 m [6]. Earlier launch planning dates of late 2023 and then 2024 have passed without a confirmed flight in the sources reviewed [6]. The mass and dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed [6]. The same spacecraft is discussed as a relay in the communication relay article (catalogue entry 177).

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: **Dimensions and proportions.** No dimensions are stated in the sources reviewed for the LuGRE payload or its receiver. The dimensions of the LRO laser ranging hardware, Moonlight and Lunar Pathfinder are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed [1][3][4][5][6].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: **Mass and weight.** The complete LuGRE flight payload is reported as under 5 kg. The receiver alone has no published mass [1]. The masses of the LRO laser ranging hardware, Moonlight and Lunar Pathfinder are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed [3][4][5][6].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: **Power requirements.** The LuGRE payload has a reported maximum operational power of 14 W [1]. The receiver's own power is not stated. No power figures are given in the sources reviewed for the LRO laser ranging hardware, Moonlight or Lunar Pathfinder [3][4][5][6].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Lunar surface and orbital ranging hardware must operate in vacuum, through wide thermal swings and, for surface assets, through the lunar day and night. LuGRE's surface operations ended when the lander lost signal on 16 March 2025, about two weeks after landing [1]. The receiver's clock had a start-up drift transient lasting roughly 10 to 15 minutes, and its frequency drift tracked temperature, so thermal control and warm-up behaviour are operational requirements for precise timing [1].

Signal strength is a second requirement. At lunar distances, Earth-orbiting navigation signals arrive weakly. LuGRE's C/N0 range of 18 to 48 dB-Hz, and its lower-than-predicted C/N0 values, show that link margin is a design concern for this class of receiver [1].

Service delivery also depends on a defined lunar geodetic system and lunar time reference, and precision depends on constellation geometry [7].
article.limitations: The specifications are payload-specific. For LuGRE, the receiver's mass, power and dimensions are not published in the text reviewed, and its pseudorange noise values are shown only as plots [1]. The flight C/N0 shortfall relative to prediction is not explained [1]. The LRO laser ranging investigation gives only a sub-meter accuracy statement and no mass, power or launch details [3]. Moonlight and Lunar Pathfinder have no verified flight data in the sources reviewed [5][6]. Lunar navigation performance also depends on the reference frame and time system, which are not part of the payload hardware [7].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: LuGRE was carried as a payload on Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost Mission 1 lander. It was launched on 15 January 2025 at 06:11 UTC [1]. It first tracked GNSS signals in lunar orbit, and pre-landing news reported a lander distance of about 401,814 km from Earth at that point [2]. The lander landed on 2 March 2025 at 08:34 UTC, and the payload was powered on less than 24 hours later [1]. Its maximum operational power was 14 W, and it operated in real-time positioning mode [1]. No separate deployment mechanism is described in the sources reviewed.
transportation_process: The LRO laser ranging hardware is carried by LRO. Its receiver telescope and fibre-optic cable are mounted on the spacecraft's high-gain antenna [3]. No further integration details are stated on the NASA page.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Moonlight and Lunar Pathfinder are intended for operation from lunar orbit, but the sources reviewed do not verify their spacecraft integration, launch vehicle or host lander [5][6].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: LuGRE and the LRO laser ranging investigation are the two flown examples in this article. Their transport and integration routes are not generalisable to other ranging systems.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: The sources reviewed do not verify compatibility of this payload class with any named lander, rover or spacecraft. Compatibility claims are therefore not made.

article.historical_significance: According to the NAVIGATION paper on LuGRE, the experiment was the first known demonstration of GNSS signal acquisition, tracking and navigation near the Moon [1]. The LRO laser ranging investigation has supported the orbiter's precise orbit determination, and its archived page is now kept for reference [3]. Moonlight and Lunar Pathfinder are in development, and the sources reviewed do not report flight results for them [4][5][6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
Several values come from search-result summaries that could not be opened in full. These are the Moonlight 10 m performance goal and 2028 target [5], the Lunar Pathfinder accuracy projection and ranging hardware [6], and the DOP and lunar time statements [7]. They should be checked against primary documents before reuse.

The LuGRE receiver's mass, power and dimensions are not stated in the text reviewed. Pseudorange noise values are plotted and not given as numbers in that text [1]. The 1.5 km and 2 m/s figures come from a pre-landing news report with no stated basis [2]. The cause of the LuGRE C/N0 shortfall is not explained [1].

The LRO laser ranging page gives no launch year, operating status, or hardware mass and power [3]. The Lunar Pathfinder launch date is not confirmed [6].

This entry overlaps with other catalogue entries. The laser ranging instrument (185), the lunar navigation receiver (176) and the radio science experiment (178) may describe similar measurements. Readers should use the entry that best matches each instrument's function.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values have query strings and fragments removed. No image objects are included in this version. A direct JPEG for the ASI Blue Ghost lander photograph was retrieved, but its source page is reachable only through a query-string URL and the caption's Earth-on-horizon detail is not visible in the retrieved image, so it was not used. Section-level image arrays are present and empty.

data_quality_notes: LuGRE receiver mass, power and dimensions are not stated in the text reviewed. The payload-level figures (under 5 kg; maximum operational power 14 W) come from the NAVIGATION paper.

LuGRE code pseudorange and carrier-phase noise are plotted in the NAVIGATION paper; the text reviewed gives only the qualitative relation (code noise roughly two orders of magnitude above carrier-phase noise).
LuGRE flight C/N0 shortfall (7 to 12 dB below prediction for GPS L1) is reported as under investigation; no cause is given.
The 1.5 km position error and 2 m/s velocity error come from a February 2025 pre-landing news report with no stated basis or conditions.
Landing site: ASI reports Mare Crisium. The ASI article's only retrieved URL carries a query string, so it is not cited, and the site is not stated in the NAVIGATION paper text reviewed.
LRO laser ranging page: launch year, current operating status, and hardware mass and power are not stated; the page is archived and marked for reference only.
Moonlight 10 m performance goal and 2028 flight-model target come from search-result summaries of a 2026 ESA and Telespazio presentation whose PDF could not be read as text in this run. Not verified.

Lunar Pathfinder: the around-100 m projection and the X-band transponder and laser retroreflector come from a search-result summary. The ESA article URL returned 404 on fetch. Launch date not confirmed.
LunaNet DOP and lunar time and geodetic-system statements come from a search-result summary of the NASA LunaNet and LCRNS briefing, which was not opened in full.
Sources marked as search-result listing or summary only were not opened in full; their figures should be checked before reuse.
